# MEMORANDUM

**To:** Supervising Partner, Project Ashgrove
**From:** Corporate Associate
**Re:** Semeith Pictures Holdings, LLC: Buyer-side issues in the Ashgrove Film Releasing stock purchase
**Documents reviewed:** All eight documents in the folder:
- Stock Purchase Agreement (SPA)
- Escrow Agreement
- Bill of Sale and Contribution Agreement
- Ventrice Executive Employment Agreement
- Transition Services Agreement (TSA)
- Deal Call Meeting Notes (March 10, 2026)
- Seller Board Consent
- Closing Funds Flow Memorandum

*Privileged and Confidential. Attorney Work Product.*

---

## Executive Summary

The deal has six substantive problems for Semeith. Several of them come from the same source. **SPA Section 11.9** provides that if the SPA conflicts with an Ancillary Agreement, *"the Ancillary Agreement governs with respect to its own subject matter."* As a result, defects in the Bill of Sale and the Escrow Agreement override the protective terms of the SPA. Two of the issues go to whether the client receives what it is paying $46,000,000 for: the narrowed Film Library and the escrow cap on carve-out claims.

| # | Issue | Primary location | Severity |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Buyer gives an uncapped indemnity for Seller Guarantees, including pre-closing obligations | SPA Art. I ("Seller Guarantees"), §§ 9.3(c), 9.5(e) | **High** |
| 2 | Bill of Sale narrows "Film Library," so the 2025 titles and the 2026 Release Slate are not conveyed | Bill of Sale §§ 1.1, 2.1; SPA §§ 1.1, 6.8, 11.9 | **High** |
| 3 | Escrow is the sole source of recovery, which caps Fraud, Fundamental Representation and Tax claims at $3,450,000 | Escrow Agt. § 7.4; SPA §§ 9.5(d), 11.9 | **High** |
| 4 | General Representations expire July 29, 2026, before the first participation statement is due | SPA §§ 9.1, 4.12; Escrow Agt. §§ 5.1, 7.1 | **High** |
| 5 | Seller may assign the TSA or delegate services, including to a competitor, without consent | TSA § 12.3 | Medium–High |
| 6 | Marisol Ventrice's change-of-control consent is not disclosed and is not a closing condition | SPA §§ 4.6, 7.2(d); Ventrice EA § 10.2 | **High** |

**Timing note:** the documents describe a March 31, 2026 Closing. Please confirm the current status of the deal.
- If Closing has not occurred, every fix below is a drafting change or a closing deliverable.
- If the documents have already been signed, Issues 2, 4 and 6 become urgent post-closing claims and remediation items. The July 29, 2026 survival date in Issue 4 may already have passed.

**Key economic reference points:**
- Purchase Price: $46,000,000 (SPA § 2.1).
- General indemnity Cap: **10% of the Purchase Price ($4,600,000)** (SPA § 9.5(a)).
- Basket: $230,000 (SPA § 9.5(b)).
- Escrow Amount: $3,450,000 (Escrow Agt. § 2.1), held by Ostrander Trust Company, N.A.
- Governing law: New York for all documents.

---

## Threshold Point: SPA Section 11.9 (Order of Precedence)

SPA § 11.9 makes each Ancillary Agreement govern its own subject matter wherever it conflicts with the SPA. "Ancillary Agreements" is defined in SPA § 1.1 to include the Escrow Agreement, the Bill of Sale and the TSA. The clause therefore works against Buyer in two places:
- The **Bill of Sale controls what is conveyed** (Issue 2).
- The **Escrow Agreement controls the source of recovery** (Issue 3).

**Recommended global fix:** Reverse the default. The SPA should prevail over any Ancillary Agreement on:
- the scope of the Film Library and the Contributed Assets;
- indemnification, survival, the Cap, the Basket and the carve-outs; and
- Buyer's remedies.

At most, an Ancillary Agreement should govern only purely mechanical matters within its scope, such as escrow disbursement procedures or TSA service levels. This fix should be made in addition to the document-specific fixes below, not instead of them.

---

## Issue 1: Uncapped Buyer Indemnity for Seller Guarantees

**Location:** SPA Article I (definition of "Seller Guarantees"); SPA § 9.3(c); SPA § 9.5(e). Related: SPA § 6.7.

**What the documents say:**
- **Definition.** "Seller Guarantees" covers every guarantee, letter of credit, keep-well, surety bond or other credit support Seller or its Affiliates gave for any Company obligation, *"whether arising before or after the Closing."* It expressly includes Seller's guarantees of the Company's minimum-guarantee payment obligations to producers and licensors.
- **§ 9.3(c).** Buyer must indemnify the Seller Indemnified Parties for all Losses arising out of any Seller Guarantee, "including any payment made or obligation incurred" by Seller under it.
- **§ 9.5(e).** The Cap, the Basket and the other limitations in Section 9.5 *"shall not apply to claims under Section 9.3(c)."* Even the mitigation and insurance offset in § 9.5(f) appears to be switched off.
- **§ 6.7.** Seller must keep the guarantees in place until they are released. Buyer only has to use commercially reasonable efforts to obtain releases. There is no outside date and no fee arrangement.

**Why it matters to Semeith:**
- Read together, these provisions make Semeith the **unlimited backstop** for every guaranty call. That includes defaults on minimum-guarantee obligations the Company incurred **before Closing, while Seller owned and controlled it**.
- Producer minimum guarantees in independent film distribution can be large and can come due over several years. An unfulfilled MG on a title that underperformed under Seller's watch would flow straight back to Buyer with no ceiling.
- The allocation is lopsided. Seller's indemnity to Buyer for pre-closing matters is capped at $4,600,000, is subject to a $230,000 Basket, and (see Issue 3) is in practice limited to the $3,450,000 escrow. Buyer's indemnity to Seller is unlimited.
- There is a further mismatch. Under Bill of Sale § 3.1, the Company assumes only Contributed Contract obligations that "first arise after the Effective Date." Yet § 9.3(c) makes Buyer indemnify Seller for guaranty payments on obligations that pre-date it.

**Recommended fix:**
1. Limit the "Seller Guarantees" indemnity in § 9.3(c) to Losses from **Company obligations first arising after the Closing**. Delete "whether arising before or after the Closing" for indemnity purposes.
2. Add an express Seller indemnity under § 9.2 for any Losses from guaranty calls relating to **pre-closing obligations, defaults or performance shortfalls**. This indemnity should not be subject to the Cap or the Basket.
3. Delete § 9.5(e), or replace it with a dedicated cap on § 9.3(c) claims. Preserve the § 9.5(f) mitigation and insurance offsets.
4. Require Seller to deliver a schedule of all existing Seller Guarantees, with amounts and maturities, as part of the Disclosure Schedule.
5. Consider an outside date for the § 6.7 release efforts, with Buyer's indemnity limited to guarantees still outstanding on that date.

---

## Issue 2: Bill of Sale Narrows "Film Library": 2025 Titles and 2026 Release Slate Not Conveyed

**Location:**
- Bill of Sale § 1.1 (definition of "Film Library") and § 2.1(a) (Conveyance); also § 2.2 (Retained Assets).
- Conflicts with SPA § 1.1 ("Film Library"), § 6.8 (Contribution of Film Library) and § 11.9.

**What the documents say:**
- **SPA § 1.1.** "Film Library" means all released and unreleased titles Seller or its Affiliates distribute, *"including the 2026 Release Slate."* The 2026 Release Slate is defined by reference to Section 1.1 of the Disclosure Schedule.
- **SPA § 6.8.** Seller must contribute "the Film Library" to the Company under the Bill of Sale no later than the Business Day before Closing.
- **Bill of Sale § 1.1** (dated March 30, 2026). The Bill of Sale redefines "Film Library" as titles *"theatrically released on or before December 31, 2024,"* plus derivative rights. Section 2.1 conveys only that narrower set.
- **Bill of Sale § 2.2.** Seller "retain[s] all assets not included in the Contributed Assets."
- **The definitions.** Bill of Sale § 1.1 says capitalized terms take their SPA meanings "unless defined" in the Bill of Sale. "Film Library" is defined there, so the narrow version controls within the Bill of Sale.

**Why it matters to Semeith:**
- Under SPA § 11.9, the Bill of Sale governs its own subject matter, which is the conveyance. The Company would therefore **not receive**:
  - titles released in calendar 2025;
  - the 2026 Release Slate; or
  - any unreleased titles.
- These are likely the most valuable and revenue-generating assets in an independent distributor's library. Semeith would pay $46,000,000 for a Company holding only the back catalog.
- The rest of the Contributed Assets fall with the definition, because they are tied to "Film Library title[s]." The Contributed Contracts, Library Receivables, Elements and Marketing Materials for 2025 and 2026 titles all stay with Seller.
- A claim under SPA § 4.10 (Film Library rep) or § 6.8 (covenant) is a weak substitute:
  - a § 4.10 claim is capped and survives only to July 29, 2026 (Issue 4);
  - recovery is confined to the escrow (Issue 3); and
  - Seller may argue that § 11.9 means there is no breach because the Bill of Sale governs.
- Bill of Sale § 6.2 states that the Bill of Sale does not expand or limit the SPA's Film Library reps. That helps only modestly.

**Recommended fix:**
1. Before signing, revise Bill of Sale § 1.1 so "Film Library" has **the meaning given in the Purchase Agreement**. Expressly include all 2025 releases, the 2026 Release Slate and all unreleased titles.
2. Reconcile Bill of Sale Schedule A with Disclosure Schedule § 4.10 and § 1.1 (2026 Release Slate) title by title before the March 30 signing. The meeting notes show Seller's counsel was to circulate Schedule A by March 20, 2026.
3. In the SPA, add language stating that the SPA definition of "Film Library" controls, notwithstanding § 11.9.
4. Use Bill of Sale § 7.2, which requires Buyer's written consent to amendments, and SPA § 7.2(b) (contribution under § 6.8 as a closing condition). Buyer should **not waive** § 7.2(b) or fund until a conforming Bill of Sale is delivered. Add "Bill of Sale conforms to SPA Film Library definition" to the funds-flow pre-funding conditions (Funds Flow § 7.1(a)).

---

## Issue 3: Escrow "Sole and Exclusive Source of Recovery" Removes the Cap Carve-Outs

**Location:** Escrow Agreement § 7.4 (Exclusive Source of Recovery). Conflicts with SPA § 9.5(d) (Carve-Outs), and § 9.6 and § 9.7 (Exclusive Remedy), through SPA § 11.9.

**What the documents say:**
- **SPA § 9.5(d).** The Cap and the Basket *"shall not apply to Losses arising from Fraud, breaches of Fundamental Representations, or Taxes."*
- **SPA § 9.6.** Indemnity amounts are to be satisfied "first" from the Escrow Funds. That wording implies recourse against Seller beyond the escrow.
- **SPA § 9.7.** Fraud claims are preserved.
- **Escrow Agreement § 7.4.** The Escrow Funds are *"the sole and exclusive source of recovery"* of the Buyer Indemnified Parties for all Losses under Article IX, *"whether or not subject to the Cap."* The section also mischaracterizes § 9.6 as contemplating payment "solely" from escrow.

**Why it matters to Semeith:**
- Through SPA § 11.9, Escrow § 7.4 overrides the SPA. Recovery for **Fraud, breaches of Fundamental Representations and Taxes** (including Seller's § 9.2(c) pre-closing tax indemnity) is limited to **$3,450,000**.
- That is **below even the general $4,600,000 Cap**. The carve-outs therefore become worse than ordinary claims.
- The Fundamental Representations include title to the Shares (§ 4.3) and Taxes (§ 4.11). These go to the core of the deal, and the SPA deliberately gave them uncapped, statute-of-limitations-length protection.
- The escrow also substantially releases on the Initial Release Date (Issue 4). After that, Seller could argue Buyer has **no source of recovery at all** for a Fraud or Fundamental Representation claim discovered later. That would gut the survival period in § 9.1.

**Recommended fix:**
1. Revise Escrow § 7.4 so the Escrow Funds are the **first, not exclusive**, source of recovery. Expressly state that nothing in the Escrow Agreement limits Buyer's direct recourse against Seller for:
   - (a) Fraud, Fundamental Representation and Tax claims;
   - (b) amounts above the Escrow Funds up to the Cap; and
   - (c) claims made after the escrow is released.
2. Correct the reference to SPA § 9.6 so it matches the SPA's "first" language.
3. Add the reversed precedence language described in the Threshold Point section, so the SPA controls on remedies and limitations.
4. Consider a separate, longer-dated escrow or holdback for Tax and Fundamental Representation exposure, or a Seller parent guaranty if Seller's creditworthiness is a concern.

---

## Issue 4: General Representations Survive Only 120 Days, Expiring Before the First Participation Statement

**Location:** SPA § 9.1 (Survival) and § 4.12 (Participations and Residuals). Escrow Agreement § 5.1 (Initial Release Date) and § 7.1 (Claim Notice window).

**What the documents say:**
- **SPA § 9.1.** The General Representations *"shall survive the Closing until the Initial Release Date."* That term is defined only in the Escrow Agreement.
- **Escrow § 5.1.** The Initial Release Date is *"120 days following the Closing Date."* From a March 31, 2026 Closing, that is **July 29, 2026**.
- **Escrow § 7.1.** Claim Notices may be delivered only "before the Initial Release Date."
- **Escrow § 5.2.** The balance, less pending claims, is released to Seller within three Business Days after the Initial Release Date.
- **SPA § 4.12.** Producer participation statements are rendered within 90 days after each June 30 and December 31. The first post-closing statement covers the period ending June 30, 2026 and is due **September 28, 2026**, roughly two months after the General Representations expire.

**Why it matters to Semeith:**
- The General Representations are the ones most likely to surface problems in a film distribution business:
  - participations and residuals accuracy (§ 4.12);
  - exhibitor and sub-distributor receivables (§ 4.12);
  - Film Library rights (§ 4.10);
  - material contracts (§ 4.9);
  - financial statements (§ 4.7); and
  - litigation (§ 4.13).
- Inaccuracies in participation accounting and exhibitor settlements typically come to light only when statements are prepared, when participants audit, or after a full accounting cycle.
- The **first participation statement under Semeith's ownership** will not be rendered until after the claims window has closed. Worse, Seller itself prepares that statement under the TSA.
- A 120-day survival period, measured from an escrow release date rather than a market survival period, gives Buyer **no practical window** to discover a breach and bring a claim. The § 4.12 rep is effectively illusory.
- Tying survival to the escrow release date also means any future change to the escrow mechanics silently shortens or lengthens SPA survival.

**Recommended fix:**
1. Amend SPA § 9.1 so the General Representations survive **at least 18 months after the Closing Date**, stated as a fixed period in the SPA and **independent of the escrow release schedule**. Delete the cross-reference to the Initial Release Date.
2. Extend the Initial Release Date to match, at least 12 to 18 months. Alternatively, use a staged release, for example 50% at 12 months and the balance at 18 months. Either way, the escrow should cover at least one full semi-annual participation cycle and a participant audit window.
3. Amend Escrow § 7.1 so Claim Notices may be delivered at any time during the applicable SPA survival period.
4. Consider a specific indemnity, outside the Cap and the Basket, for pre-closing participation and residual underpayments, with a longer survival period. Participant audit rights often run three or more years.

---

## Issue 5: One-Sided TSA Assignment: Seller May Assign or Delegate to a Competitor

**Location:** TSA § 12.3 (Assignment).

**What the TSA says:**
- Recipient (the Company) may not assign without Provider's prior written consent.
- Provider *"may assign this Agreement, or delegate the performance of any Service, in whole or in part, to any Person without the consent of Recipient."*
- There is no restriction on assignment to a competitor, and no termination right for Recipient if an assignment occurs.
- Recipient may terminate individual Services for convenience on 30 days' notice (§ 9.2). That notice period is a slow, partial remedy and leaves the Company without critical services mid-transition.

**Why it matters to Semeith:**
- The Services cover theatrical booking, participation accounting and digital cinema delivery (TSA § 3.1). Performing them requires access to the Company's most sensitive commercial information, which TSA § 1.1 itself classes as Confidential Information:
  - exhibitor terms;
  - film rental and settlement data;
  - release calendars;
  - booking strategies; and
  - participation data.
- Seller could hand all of that to a **competing distributor**, or delegate booking for the 2026 slate to one. The TSA confidentiality clause (§ 8) binds only "the parties."
- Provider also collects film rentals in trust (§ 6.1). An unvetted assignee would be handling Company cash.
- Service quality during the 9-month Term (§ 2.1) could degrade if services move to a party with no history with the Company. That would undercut the § 3.2 Service Standard, which is benchmarked to Seller's own past performance.

**Recommended fix:** Revise TSA § 12.3 to:
1. Require Recipient's **prior written consent** for any assignment by Provider and any delegation or subcontracting of a Service. Limited exceptions could cover named, pre-approved vendors, such as existing delivery vendors on Schedule A.
2. **Prohibit** assignment or delegation to any competitor of the Company or Buyer, meaning any Person engaged in theatrical or digital distribution of motion pictures, in all cases.
3. Keep Provider **fully liable** for any permitted delegate. Require each delegate to sign confidentiality and data-security terms at least as protective as TSA §§ 7 and 8.
4. Give Recipient (and Buyer, as third-party beneficiary under § 12.9) an **immediate right to terminate** the TSA or any affected Service on any assignment or change of control of Provider, with full migration assistance under § 4.
5. Make assignment mutual. At a minimum, allow Recipient to assign to Buyer, its Affiliates or a successor to the Company's business without consent.

---

## Issue 6: Ventrice Change-of-Control Consent Not Disclosed and Not a Closing Condition

**Location:**
- SPA § 4.6 (Consents) and § 7.2(d) (closing condition). Related: SPA § 6.3.
- Ventrice Executive Employment Agreement § 10.2 (Consent; Effect of Change of Control), § 10.1 and § 6.3.

**What the documents say:**
- **SPA § 4.6.** Seller represents that *"No consent, approval or waiver of any Person"* is required other than Kestrelwave Streaming, Inc.'s consent under its output agreement.
- **SPA § 7.2(d).** This conditions Closing only on the Kestrelwave consent. **The SPA's closing conditions do not require Ms. Ventrice's consent.**
- **SPA § 6.3.** Seller's efforts covenant extends only to the § 4.6 consent.
- **Ventrice EA § 10.1(a).** A "Change of Control" includes any sale of more than 50% of the Company's voting stock. The sale of 100% of the Shares to Semeith is squarely within this.
- **Ventrice EA § 10.2.** The Company *"shall not undergo a Change of Control without the Executive's prior written consent."* If a Change of Control occurs without that consent:
  - **(a)** it is automatically Good Reason. She may resign within 90 days, with no notice or cure;
  - **(b)** she receives a lump-sum severance of **24 months' Base Salary**, which is $850,000 at the $425,000 rate, plus a pro-rated target bonus and 12 months of COBRA; and
  - **(c)** all of the Company's rights in the **Executive Titles revert to her**. This covers distribution rights, Elements, marketing materials and future revenue. The Company must deliver all materials within 30 days.

**Why it matters to Semeith:**
- Closing as currently papered would **breach** the employment agreement and trigger all of these remedies. The risks are:
  - loss of the Company's President at the moment of transition;
  - an $850,000+ cash severance obligation borne by the Company, which is now Buyer's; and
  - **loss of a portion of the Film Library**. The Executive Titles are titles she sourced, potentially including recent and slate titles.
- Under Ventrice EA § 9.3, she is free to exploit reverted rights despite her non-interference covenant.
- The reversion directly cuts into the asset base Semeith is paying for, and compounds Issue 2.
- Buyer's only recourse would be a claim for breach of § 4.6, § 4.5(c) or § 4.9. That claim is capped, expires July 29, 2026, and is confined to the escrow (Issues 3 and 4).
- Nothing else in the folder covers this gap:
  - the funds flow pre-funding conditions (Funds Flow § 7.1(b)) track only the Kestrelwave consent;
  - the March 10 deal call notes (Item 6) discuss only Kestrelwave; and
  - the Seller Board Consent (§ 4.4) authorizes "any other consent" but does not identify this one.

**Recommended fix:**
1. Amend SPA § 4.6 to disclose the Ventrice consent requirement under Ventrice EA § 10.2. Extend the § 6.3 efforts covenant to cover it.
2. Add a new **closing condition in SPA § 7.2** requiring delivery of Ms. Ventrice's written consent to the Change of Control, together with an express **waiver** of:
   - her Good Reason right under § 10.2(a);
   - the 24-month severance under § 10.2(b); and
   - the Executive Titles reversion under § 10.2(c).
   The consent and waiver should be in a form reasonably satisfactory to Buyer and signed so as to satisfy Ventrice EA § 11.4. Add it to the Seller deliveries in § 3.2 and to Funds Flow § 7.1.
3. Obtain Exhibit A (Executive Titles) now, as updated under Ventrice EA § 6.2. Cross-check it against the Film Library schedules to size the exposure.
4. Add a **specific Seller indemnity**, outside the Cap, the Basket and the escrow-only limitation, for any Losses under Ventrice EA § 10.2 if the consent is defective or later challenged.
5. Commercially, the client should decide whether to sign a new or amended employment agreement or retention arrangement with Ms. Ventrice at Closing. Also check § 10.3 (the 280G cutback) for interaction with any new arrangement.

---

## Other Observations (No Additional Action Required Unless Noted)

- **Distractor documents.** The Deal Call Notes, Seller Board Consent and Closing Funds Flow Memorandum are consistent with the deal terms:
  - $46,000,000 price;
  - $3,450,000 escrow;
  - $42,550,000 to Seller;
  - March 31, 2026 Closing;
  - Ostrander as Escrow Agent;
  - 9-month TSA; and
  - New York law.

  They raise no independent issues. They should be updated to reflect the fixes above, in particular the Funds Flow § 7.1 pre-funding conditions (conforming Bill of Sale; Ventrice consent and waiver).
- **Escrow Agreement § 8.4.** Buyer and Seller are jointly and severally liable to indemnify the Escrow Agent. This is market and acceptable, given the 50/50 allocation between the parties.
- **Seller creditworthiness.** If Issues 1 and 3 are fixed by restoring direct recourse against Seller, confirm Seller's ability to pay post-closing. Consider a parent guaranty.

---

## Recommended Next Steps

1. **Before any signing or funding:** deliver Buyer's markup covering:
   - SPA §§ 1.1, 4.6, 6.3, 6.7, 7.2, 9.1, 9.2, 9.3(c), 9.5(e) and 11.9;
   - Escrow Agreement §§ 5.1, 7.1 and 7.4;
   - Bill of Sale § 1.1 and Schedule A; and
   - TSA § 12.3.
2. **Do not waive** SPA § 7.2(b) until the Bill of Sale conveys the full SPA-defined Film Library.
3. **Request** the following from Seller:
   - Ventrice Exhibit A;
   - the Seller Guarantee schedule; and
   - Disclosure Schedule §§ 1.1 and 4.10.
4. **Client call:** discuss with Semeith:
   - the Ventrice retention strategy; and
   - its risk appetite on the Seller Guarantee exposure, including MG amounts outstanding by title.
5. **If Closing has already occurred:**
   - immediately assess whether any Claim Notice was served before July 29, 2026;
   - evaluate claims based on the Bill of Sale shortfall and the Ventrice consent; and
   - preserve all rights under SPA §§ 9.7 and 11.10.

**What the documents say:**
- **SPA definition.** SPA §1.1 defines "Film Library" as *all* released and unreleased titles Seller or its Affiliates distribute, *"including the 2026 Release Slate."*
- **SPA §6.8.** Seller must contribute the Film Library to the Company before Closing by the Bill of Sale.
- **Bill of Sale definition.** The Bill of Sale is dated March 30, 2026. Its §1.1 redefines "Film Library" as titles *"theatrically released on or before December 31, 2024,"* plus derivative rights in those titles.
- **Bill of Sale §2.1.** Section 2.1 conveys only that narrower set.
- **Bill of Sale §2.2.** Section 2.2 confirms that Seller retains everything else.
- **Order of precedence.** SPA §11.9 makes the Bill of Sale control its own subject matter, which is the conveyance.

**Why it matters to Semeith:**
- As drafted, the Company, and therefore Buyer, would **not acquire**:
  - any title released in 2025;
  - any unreleased title; or
  - the 2026 Release Slate.
- These are likely the most valuable, revenue-generating assets supporting the $46,000,000 price.
- Related contracts, receivables and Elements also stay with Seller, because the definitions of "Contributed Contracts," "Library Receivables" and "Elements" are keyed to Film Library titles.
- A post-closing claim is a poor substitute for fixing the document:
  - Buyer could argue breach of §6.8 or of the §4.10 Film Library representation.
  - §4.10 is a General Representation. It is subject to the $4,600,000 Cap and survives only until the Initial Release Date (see Issue 3).
  - Seller will point to §11.9 and to Bill of Sale §6.2.
- There is also closing-condition risk. §7.2(b) conditions Closing on "the contribution under Section 6.8." Delivery of a nonconforming Bill of Sale should mean the condition is not satisfied. However, the funds flow memo (§7.1(a)) treats mere execution and delivery of the Bill of Sale as the pre-funding trigger, so the condition could be overlooked.

**Recommended fix:**
1. Revise Bill of Sale §1.1 to adopt the SPA definition verbatim, for example: "'Film Library' has the meaning given in the Purchase Agreement." Confirm that Schedule A lists every 2025 title and every 2026 Release Slate title, matching Disclosure Schedule §§1.1 and 4.10.
2. Amend SPA §11.9 so that the SPA's definitions and §6.8 control over any Ancillary Agreement on the scope of assets conveyed.
3. Use Bill of Sale §7.2, which requires Buyer's written consent to any amendment before Closing, to make sure no version is signed without our sign-off. Add the form of Bill of Sale as an exhibit to the SPA.
4. Make the §4.10 representation (title to the Film Library as defined in the SPA) a Fundamental Representation, or carve it out of the Cap and the short survival period.
5. Update funds flow memo §7.1(a) so that Buyer confirms the Bill of Sale conforms to the SPA before any wire is released.

## Issue 3: General Representations Expire Before Breaches Can Be Discovered

**Where:**
- SPA §9.1 (Survival) and §4.12 (Participations and Residuals)
- Escrow Agreement §5.1 (Initial Release Date); related: Escrow Agreement §7.1

**What the documents say:**
- **Survival period.** SPA §9.1: the General Representations *"shall survive the Closing until the Initial Release Date."*
- **Initial Release Date.** Escrow Agreement §5.1 sets the Initial Release Date at *"120 days following the Closing Date."*
- **Resulting expiry.** From a March 31, 2026 Closing, that is **July 29, 2026**.
- **Claim window.** Escrow Agreement §7.1 also allows Claim Notices only before the Initial Release Date.
- **Statement timing.** SPA §4.12 states that producer participation statements are rendered within 90 days after each June 30 and December 31. The first post-closing statement (for the period ending June 30, 2026) is therefore due by **September 28, 2026**, about two months *after* the General Representations expire.

**Why it matters to Semeith:**
- The key operational representations are all General Representations. These include participations and residuals (§4.12), exhibitor and sub-distributor receivables (§4.12), material contracts (§4.9), financial statements (§4.7) and Film Library title (§4.10).
- Inaccuracies in participation accounting, receivables and exhibitor settlements typically surface through the statement cycle, participant audits and year-end close. None of these will happen within 120 days.
- In practice, Buyer would have **no usable window** to discover breaches and bring claims. This also weakens the remedy in Issues 1 and 2.
- Seller will also be performing participation accounting under the TSA during this period. That makes it even less likely Buyer will independently spot pre-closing errors before the claim window closes.
- Tying survival to an escrow release date allows the escrow mechanics to set Buyer's substantive rights.

**Recommended fix:**
1. Amend SPA §9.1 so the General Representations survive for **at least 18 months after Closing**, as a fixed period stated in the SPA and not linked to the escrow release schedule.
2. Consider a longer period, or treatment as a Fundamental Representation, for §4.12 (participations and residuals) and §4.10 (Film Library).
3. Conform the escrow:
   - extend the Initial Release Date in Escrow Agreement §5.1 to match the survival period, or at minimum to a date after the second post-closing statement cycle (around March 2027); and
   - revise Escrow Agreement §7.1 so the timing of Claim Notices does not cut off SPA claims.
4. Confirm that a claim noticed within the survival period survives until resolved, which SPA §9.1 already provides.

## Issue 4: Seller May Freely Assign the TSA or Delegate Services (Including to a Competitor)

**Where:** TSA §12.3 (Assignment)

**What the documents say:**
- **Recipient.** The Company, as Recipient, may not assign the TSA without Provider's (Seller's) prior written consent.
- **Provider.** Seller, as Provider, *"may assign this Agreement, or delegate the performance of any Service, in whole or in part, to any Person without the consent of Recipient."*
- **No exit for Recipient.** The TSA gives Recipient no termination right on an assignment or delegation by Provider.

**Why it matters to Semeith:**
- The three Services run for 9 months after Closing (TSA §2.1) and are core to the business: theatrical booking, participation accounting, and digital cinema delivery.
- Performing them requires access to the Company's most sensitive information, including exhibitor terms, film rental and settlement data, release calendars, booking strategies and participant data. The TSA's own definition of Confidential Information lists this material.
- Seller could transfer the TSA, or any part of it, to a **competing distributor** or to an untested vendor. That party would gain this information and control over the Company's day-to-day releases.
- TSA §8 limits use of Confidential Information. It does not prevent a competitor from receiving the information in the first place.
- Buyer's remedies would be weak:
  - TSA §10.2 caps liability at the Service Fees.
  - Termination for breach (§9.3) is unavailable, because an assignment is expressly permitted.
- The clause is also one-sided. Buyer cannot even assign to an Affiliate without Seller's consent.

**Recommended fix:**
1. Revise §12.3 to require **Recipient's prior written consent** for any assignment by Provider or delegation of any Service. Allow a narrow exception for delegation to named subcontractors already on Schedule A.
2. Add an express **prohibition on assignment or delegation to any competitor** of the Company, or to any Person engaged in theatrical or digital distribution of motion pictures.
3. Give Recipient the right to **terminate the TSA or any affected Service** on notice, without penalty, if Provider assigns, delegates, or undergoes a change of control. Provider should owe migration assistance and delivery of Recipient Data on that termination.
4. Make Provider liable for any permitted subcontractor as for itself. Require subcontractors to accept the TSA §7 and §8 obligations in writing.
5. Make the clause mutual: allow Recipient to assign to Buyer, its Affiliates, or a successor to the Company's business without consent.

## Issue 5: Undisclosed Change-of-Control Consent Right of the Company's President

**Where:**
- SPA §4.6 (Consents) and §7.2(d) (closing condition)
- Ventrice Executive Employment Agreement §10.1, §10.2; related: §7.4(e), §8.2

**What the documents say:**
- **SPA §4.6.** Seller represents that *"No consent, approval or waiver of any Person"* is required for the transaction other than Kestrelwave Streaming, Inc.'s consent under its output agreement.
- **SPA §7.2(d).** This section conditions Closing **only** on the Kestrelwave consent.
- **SPA §6.3.** Seller's consent-efforts covenant also covers only the §4.6 consent.
- **Ventrice §10.1(a).** A sale of more than 50% of the Company's voting stock is a "Change of Control." The sale of 100% of the Shares is squarely within this.
- **Ventrice §10.2.** The Company *"shall not undergo a Change of Control without the Executive's prior written consent."* If a Change of Control occurs without that consent:
  - (a) it constitutes Good Reason, and Ms. Ventrice may resign within 90 days without the usual notice and cure process;
  - (b) she receives a lump-sum severance of **24 months' Base Salary** (at least $850,000 at the $425,000 rate). This is in addition to a pro-rated target bonus (50% of base) and 12 months of COBRA, and it is subject only to a release; and
  - (c) all of the Company's rights in the **Executive Titles** revert to her. These include distribution rights, Elements, marketing materials and post-resignation revenue.
- **Surviving rights.** Her 1% acquisition incentive (§4.3) also survives any termination other than for Cause.

**Why it matters to Semeith:**
- The SPA neither discloses this consent nor requires it. As drafted, **Buyer would be obliged to close without it.** Neither the deal call notes (§6) nor the funds flow memo (§7.1(b)) tracks it; both refer only to Kestrelwave.
- Buyer would inherit significant cash exposure and, more importantly, the risk of losing library titles the President sourced. That would cut into the Film Library Buyer is paying for.
- The Executive Titles are listed on Exhibit A, which was not in the folder. We cannot yet quantify how much of the library is affected.
- Loss of the President would also disrupt the business during the TSA transition.
- An indemnity claim for breach of §4.6 is not an adequate remedy. §4.6 is a General Representation, subject to the $4,600,000 Cap and the 120-day survival problem (Issue 3).
- Seller's board consent (§4.4) authorizes Seller's officers to obtain "any other consent." Seller therefore has authority to seek this consent and simply has not.

**Recommended fix:**
1. Require Seller to amend §4.6 and the Disclosure Schedule to disclose the Ventrice §10.2 consent requirement.
2. Add a new Buyer closing condition in §7.2: delivery of Ms. Ventrice's **written consent to the transaction and an irrevocable waiver** of her rights under §10.2(a)–(c) arising from it. Extend §6.3 and §3.2(f) to cover it, and add it to funds flow memo §7.1(b).
3. Ideally, obtain an amendment to her agreement deleting the consent right and the title reversion going forward. Consider pairing it with a retention arrangement Buyer is comfortable with.
4. As a backstop, add a **specific, uncapped Seller indemnity** under §9.2 for any severance, reversion or other Losses under Ventrice §10.2 arising from this transaction, with survival matching the 90-day resignation window plus a claims period.
5. Obtain and review Exhibit A (Executive Titles) and cross-check it against Bill of Sale Schedule A and Disclosure Schedule §4.10.
